title: QB or Offensive Line? The real reason your favorite team is bad
text:
2025, just like any other NFL season, kept the theme of o-line play being a major reason why every single team over- or underperformed. Which is shocking because there are another 17 players on the field at any given point. With offensive line statistics being very arbitrary and hard to find, this allows people and fans to be able to continue to complain about this without actually being held accountable for their reasoning behind it. One of the only ways that I could find to take into account the play of these big men, while taking out the scale of strength of schedule, is by using PFF’s (somewhat skewed) ratings for every single team.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)

teamolinerating <- read_csv("Data/Team Ratings.csv")
PatriotsOL <- teamolinerating |> filter(Team == "Patriots") 
CowboysOL <- teamolinerating |> filter(Team == "Cowboys")
SeahawksOL <- teamolinerating |> filter(Team == "Seahawks") 
RamsOL <- teamolinerating |> filter(Team == "Rams")
LionsOL <- teamolinerating |> filter(Team == "Lions") 
NinersOL <- teamolinerating |> filter(Team == "49ers")
BillsOL <- teamolinerating |> filter(Team == "Bills")
 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_bar(data=teamolinerating, aes(x=reorder(Team,Rating), weight=Rating), fill= "lightgray",)+
  geom_bar(data=PatriotsOL, aes(x=reorder(Team,Rating), weight=Rating), fill= "#002244")+
  geom_bar(data=SeahawksOL, aes(x=reorder(Team,Rating), weight=Rating), fill= "#69BE28")+
  geom_bar(data=BillsOL, aes(x=reorder(Team,Rating), weight=Rating), fill= "#00338D")+
  geom_bar(data=RamsOL, aes(x=reorder(Team,Rating), weight=Rating), fill= "#003594")+
  geom_bar(data=LionsOL, aes(x=reorder(Team,Rating), weight=Rating), fill= "#0076b6")+
  geom_bar(data=NinersOL, aes(x=reorder(Team,Rating), weight=Rating), fill= "#B3995D")+
  geom_bar(data=CowboysOL, aes(x=reorder(Team,Rating), weight=Rating), fill= "#041E42")+
  coord_flip()+
  geom_hline(yintercept = 66.05,color="black")+
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept=66.05)) +
  geom_text(aes(0,70,label = "66.05", vjust = -1))+
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 80), breaks = seq(0, 80, by = 20))+
   labs(
    x=" ", 
    y="PFF 2026 Team Oline Rating", 
    title="Does a better Oline equal a better passing offense?", 
    subtitle="The Superbowl teams appear on both sides of the mean, but five of the \nbest seven passing offenses sit at or below the average rating.", 
    caption="Source: Pro Footbal Focus| By Ethan Warren"
    ) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 8), 
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size=10), 
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title.position = "plot"
    ) 









So the offensive line means nothing in terms of how well an offense plays, done deal. The Super Bowl-winning Seahawks offense that scored the third-most points per game and eighth-most passing yards didn’t need an offensive line to win it all. In a vacuum, this statistic alone can give us a little bit of insight into how a team is built, but it can also be very important in looking at how a playbook is built. San Francisco, for instance, suffered another year of all-around injuries that meant that nine different players at least started a game in front of the ever-mobile Brock Purdy. Speaking of Brock Purdy, how does a player and how they play take into account how an o-line plays, naturally a o-line that is more mobile will be harder to block for, in turn meaning a grade would likely be lower. Maybe a QB like Matthew Stafford standing in the pocket at one of the highest rates of any qb means they are more likely to play worse because they have to block more.


Code
QBdata <- read_csv("Data/QB Data with Oline ratings.csv")

sanders <- QBdata |> filter(QB == "Shedeur Sanders")
nine <- QBdata |> filter(QB == "JJ McCarthy")
maye <- QBdata |> filter(QB == "Drake Maye")
stafford <- QBdata |> filter(QB == "Matthew Stafford")
Flacco <- QBdata |> filter(QB == "Browns Joe Flacco")
joe2021 <- QBdata |> filter(QB == "2021 Joe Burrow")
nowheresaguy <- QBdata |> filter(QB == "Patrick Mahomes")
bigcbrock <- QBdata |> filter(QB == "Brock Purdy")


ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = QBdata,aes(x=`Oline Rating`, y=QBR, size= .75), color= "gray", alpha = .5) +
    geom_point(data = sanders,aes(x=`Oline Rating`, y=QBR, size= .75), color= "#ff3c00") +
  geom_point(data = nine,aes(x=`Oline Rating`, y=QBR, size= .75), color= "#4F2683") +
  geom_point(data = maye,aes(x=`Oline Rating`, y=QBR, size= .75), color= "#002244") +
  geom_point(data = stafford,aes(x=`Oline Rating`, y=QBR, size= .75), color= "#003594") +
  geom_point(data = Flacco,aes(x=`Oline Rating`, y=QBR, size= .75), color= "#ff3c00") +
  geom_point(data = joe2021,aes(x=`Oline Rating`, y=QBR, size= .75), color= "#fb4f14")+
  geom_point(data = nowheresaguy,aes(x=`Oline Rating`, y=QBR, size= .75), color= "#E31837")+
  geom_point(data = bigcbrock,aes(x=`Oline Rating`, y=QBR, size= .75), color= "#B3995D")+
  geom_text(data=sanders, aes(x=`Oline Rating`- 3, y=QBR+3, label=QB))+
  geom_text(data=nine, aes(x=`Oline Rating`-2, y=QBR +4, label=QB))+
  geom_text(data=maye, aes(x=`Oline Rating`-1, y=QBR-3, label=QB))+
  geom_text(data=stafford, aes(x=`Oline Rating`+1.5, y=QBR-3, label=QB))+
  geom_text(data=Flacco, aes(x=`Oline Rating`+2, y=QBR+3.2, label=QB))+
  geom_text(data=nowheresaguy, aes(x=`Oline Rating`-2, y=QBR-2, label=QB))+
  geom_text(data=joe2021, aes(x=`Oline Rating`-2, y=QBR-2, label=QB))+
  geom_text(data=bigcbrock, aes(x=`Oline Rating`, y=QBR+2.8, label=QB))+
 labs(
    x="PFF Team Offensive Rating", 
    y="ESPN's QBR rating (0-100)", 
    title="Drake `Drake Maye` Maye is pretty good at football", 
    subtitle="The Patriots QB benefited from a top 10 Oline, in turn he scored the \nhighest QBR of any Quarterback in the 2025-26 season.", 
    caption="Source: Pro Footbal Focus and Pro Football Reference | By Ethan Warren"
    ) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 8), 
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size=10), 
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title.position = "plot"
    ) 









Oh, so technically we can say that a mobile QB is harder to block for, given two of the most play-extending quarterbacks in the NFL cluster in the 55-60 level for offensive line grade while sitting in the top ten in QBR.
However, if you thought a Nebraska fan would ignore the elephant in the room, you would be very mistaken. Shedeur Sanders, who has been notoriously defended by his fan base that his coach, wide receivers, and especially the offensive line was attempting to push the fifth-round pick out of his starting position after Dillon Gabriel and Joe Flacco both moved out of the way for his Legendary heiness himself. Coming in with the fourth-highest offensive line PFF rating of any QB that started more than four games, Sanders sits as the only QB with a QBR under 30. Two other QBs that performed poorly are teammate Dillon Gabriel (31.4) and the Vikings’ JJ McCarthy, who put up a 35.6 QBR with the best o-line rating for any QB.


Code
notable <- QBdata |> 
  filter(QB == "Shedeur Sanders" |  QB == "JJ McCarthy" | QB == "Drake Maye" | QB == "Matthew Stafford" |
           QB == "Browns Joe Flacco" | QB == "2021 Joe Burrow" | QB == "Patrick Mahomes" | QB == "Brock Purdy" )
notableplus <- notable |> 
  filter(QB == "Drake Maye" | QB == "Matthew Stafford" | QB == "2021 Joe Burrow" | QB == "Patrick Mahomes" | QB == "Brock Purdy" )
notableminus <- QBdata |> 
  filter(QB == "Shedeur Sanders" |  QB == "JJ McCarthy" | QB == "Browns Joe Flacco")


ggplot() + 
  geom_segment(
    data=notable, 
    aes(
      y=reorder(QB, `Oline Rating`), yend=QB,
        x=`Oline Rating`, xend=QBR),
    color="grey",
    linewidth = 3
  )  + 
  geom_point(
    data=notable,
    aes(
      y=QB,
      x=`Oline Rating`,
      color="PFF Oline Rating"
    ),
    size=4
  ) + 
  geom_point(
    data=notableplus,
    aes(
      y=QB,
      x=`QBR`,
      color="QBR > Oline Rating"
    ),
    size=4
  ) + 
  geom_point(
    data=notableminus,
    aes(
      y=QB,
      x=`QBR`,
      color="QBR < Oline Rating"
    ),
    size=4
  ) + 
  
  scale_color_manual(name="Oline Rating", values=c("black", "red", "green"))+
  
 labs(
    x="PFF Team Offensive Rating", 
    y="ESPN's QBR rating (0-100)", 
    title="The Oline is not the reason Mr.Legendary is a bad QB", 
    subtitle="Despite what his fans say, Shedeur Sanders has just below one of the best olines during his \nstarts, But also has statistically the worst QB Rates of any qualifying QB in the NFL in 2025.", 
    caption="Source: Pro Footbal Focus and Pro Football Reference | By Ethan Warren"
    ) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 8), 
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size=10), 
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title.position = "plot"
    ) 









All in all, the o-line can play a big part in why a team struggles to put points on the board and wins on the table. At the end of the day, good QBs are going to be able to overplay the worst o-linemen, even to the level of getting sacked nine times in the Super Bowl, and still being just 3 points away from hoisting the Lombardi.
